# Abstract

This lecture surveys some of the key economic forces that have shaped the current boom in AI in general, and music AI more specifically. The first part of the lecture highlights four tendencies in particular that have laid the groundwork for the post-2020 takeoff of commercial music AI services:

* monetary policies enacted after the 2008 financial crisis, and their impact in the nature and amount of investment in music technology companies; 
* the growing importance of assetization to the post-2008 global economy, as evinced by the transformation of music rights into a prized asset class; 
* the longer-term trend within the global economy towards slowing productivity – what certain economists have dubbed “secular stagnation” – a tendency for which AI is cast as a potential solution; and
* the various forms of scarcity that afflict the AI sector, from chip shortages to the scarcities of listener time and attention that a mounting glut of AI-generated music have exacerbated.

The second and third parts of the lecture then traces how these conditions have played out in connection to the emergence and rapid growth of a number of companies specializing in music AI since 2022. First, the near zero-interest rate monetary policy pursued by the US Federal Reserve helped fuel the growth of platform monopolies across the 2010s and 2020s. On the one hand this process of platformization was critical for the mass aggregation of music and users, which AI companies were then able to exploit as a ready source of training data. On the other hand these services provided a business model that would be emulated by music AI startups like Suno and Udio, which have likewise adopted key features of the platform, including its use of subscriptions to lock users into a durable relation of dependance. Second, music AI companies have been obliged to insert themselves within a series of asset chains, which they both rest upon and further extend. Upstream, these asset chains include the computational resources and technologies they rely upon to run their systems, as well as the pools of music assets they either license or expropriate to feed these systems. But generative music systems in particular also produce downstream assets, though their legal standing and by extension their economic value is tenuous: the fact that in many jurisdictions music substantially generated using AI does not qualify for copyright protection means that when such music posted to commercial services, it is under constant threat of takedown – when it isn’t blocked from upload in the first place. Nevertheless, the relative ease with which AI filters can be skirted means that a growing number of AI-generated tracks are behaving as assets, generating revenue for their creators, even if their legal status is uncertain.

Third, while AI’s promise of overcoming secular stagnation and reversing declining productivity rates has yet to be realized, one thing the technology has accomplished in the world of music is intensifying the ongoing overproduction of music, adding to the growing glut of recorded music that saturates most online music platforms. As long-established studies of the creative industries have underscored, overproduction is a rational response to a market defined by exceedingly high levels of demand uncertainty (as is the case for the market for recorded music). But what may be a rational response at the level of the individual may result in a host of negative externalities at the level of the collective. Fourth, despite the fact that most music AI companies have adopted a platform model, the underlying dynamics of the AI sector means that they have been obliged to break with the post-scarcity economics of music streaming. Instead, the resource constraints these companies face are increasingly passed along to their consumers, in the form of fixed allowances of tokens or credits. Yet generative music companies are also responsible for exacerbating another kind of scarcity, that of audience attention, given the way their output is currently flooding the market for recorded music.

The lecture concludes by considering the interaction of these forces more holistically. One thing such a perspective underlines is the dependence of music AI companies on the broader musical commons. In particular, by modeling this commons, albeit in a partial and distorted manner, commercial music AI firms seek to transform this public resource into a privately-held asset, what might be described as commons capital. At the same time, because these firms are thoroughly intertwined with online music production and distribution networks, the music they generate imperils the commons on which they depend. If in the case of LLMs and other ML models there is a risk of model collapse, with variance diminishing and homogeneity increasing as generative outputs are fed back in as inputs for training, in the case of musical culture there is a parallel risk of commons collapse, as more and more AI generated music finds its way into the feeds and playlists of listeners, into their ears, and from there into the wider musical commons whose substance and character it may reshape in subtle yet powerful ways.
